summary: Conceptual (non-algebraic) orbital mechanics for ages 12-13. The core, counter-intuitive idea: an orbit is CONTINUOUS FREEFALL — a satellite is always falling toward the planet, but it moves sideways so fast that the curved ground falls away beneath it just as fast, so it keeps missing. Newton's cannonball thought experiment is the canonical bridge (fire faster from a mountaintop: crash → suborbital arc → circular orbit → ellipse → escape, all from one speed variable). Build two further ideas: a gravity assist (a spacecraft borrows a tiny amount of a planet's orbital momentum in a close flyby to gain speed), and the qualitative heart of the rocket equation (because a rocket must carry fuel it hasn't burned yet, propellant needed rises steeply/exponentially as demanded speed change increases). Frame throughout as momentum-versus-gravity and 'falling sideways', reserving maths for later.
misconceptions: 'There's no gravity in space, that's why astronauts float' — gravity in low orbit is nearly as strong as on the ground; they float because they and their ship are falling together
'Rockets need to keep their engines on to stay in orbit' — once at orbital speed, no thrust is needed; the craft coasts in freefall indefinitely
'Orbits are perfect circles' — most are ellipses; a circle is just the special case of exactly the right speed
'Going up is the hard part of reaching orbit' — the real challenge is going sideways fast enough; altitude alone gives you a suborbital hop that falls back down
'A gravity assist gets energy from nothing' — the craft borrows orbital momentum from the planet, which loses an unmeasurably tiny amount in exchange
'More speed just needs proportionally more fuel' — because you must carry the fuel you haven't burned, required fuel rises exponentially with desired speed change

activities.title: Newton's cannonball: one speed dial from crash to escape
steps: Stand a cannon on a mountaintop above a round planet and set a single SPEED value, then fire and watch where the projectile goes.
At low speed, observe the cannonball arc down and crash into the ground; raise the speed and watch the arc get longer but still fall back.

Keep raising the speed until you find the setting where the ball curves downward exactly as fast as the planet's surface curves away, so it sweeps all the way around into a circular orbit (and would come back and hit the cannon from behind).
Push past that setting to see the circle stretch into an ellipse, then push higher still to watch the ball escape and not return.

Compare the orbit against a faint 'no-gravity straight line' overlay showing the path the ball would take with gravity switched off, and note how far it 'falls away' from that straight line each second.
State in your own words why the orbiting ball is still falling even though it never hits the ground.
activities.insight: Orbiting is just falling and continuously missing the ground: one launch speed, varied smoothly, produces crash, circular orbit, ellipse and escape; gravity bends the would-be straight-line path into the orbit.

activities.title: The momentum-vs-gravity tug-of-war
steps: For a chosen launch, sketch or identify two arrows at the projectile: a forward (sideways) velocity arrow and an inward arrow pointing at the planet's centre for gravity.
Predict, before firing, whether a given speed will crash, circle, stretch into an ellipse or escape, and justify using the two arrows.

Explain why 'too slow' falls back and crashes, why a bit faster than circular speed stretches the orbit into an ellipse, why 'much too fast' (at or above escape speed) flies away, and what 'just right' for a circle means.
State explicitly that gravity is the only force acting on the ball in flight (in this idealised model) — there is no outward force holding it out.
activities.insight: An orbit results from sideways momentum plus a single inward gravitational pull that continually curves the path; there is no real outward force balancing gravity.

activities.title: Gravity assist: borrowing a planet's motion
steps: Time a close flyby of a spacecraft past a MOVING planet and watch a speed readout before and after the encounter.
Experiment with the timing/geometry of the flyby to make the craft gain speed, and describe what happened to its path.
Explain where the extra speed comes from — the craft borrows a tiny share of the planet's orbital momentum, while the planet loses an unmeasurably tiny amount.
Optionally, discuss with a mission navigator planning a probe to Jupiter why it might slingshot past Venus and Earth first instead of flying straight there.
activities.insight: A gravity assist is not free energy from nothing: a spacecraft exchanges momentum with a moving planet during a close flyby, gaining useful speed while the planet's change is imperceptible.

activities.title: Fuel to carry fuel: why rockets are mostly propellant
steps: Set a target speed change (Δv) and watch the required propellant amount build up.

Increase the target Δv in steps and observe that the propellant needed grows faster than in proportion — doubling the demand always takes more than double the fuel, and far more than double once the Δv is large.
Explain in your own words why this happens: the rocket must lift and accelerate the fuel it hasn't burned yet, so extra fuel also needs its own fuel to be carried.
Describe why this means getting to orbit is hard and why large rockets are mostly fuel by mass.
activities.insight: Because a rocket carries its unburned fuel, the propellant needed rises steeply (exponentially) with the demanded speed change — the qualitative heart of the rocket equation.

activities.title: Consolidate and predict
steps: Order a set of launch outcomes (crash, suborbital arc, circular orbit, ellipse, escape) from slowest to fastest launch speed.
Set the speed that produces a circular orbit and justify the choice.
Answer 'why do astronauts float?' and explain why it is freefall, not absent gravity.
Explain why a spacecraft already at orbital speed does not need its engines running to stay up.
activities.insight: Learners can apply the falling-sideways model to new cases: predicting outcomes by speed, and explaining floating and engine-off coasting.

checkQuestion: Astronauts on the Space Station float around, and the Station keeps circling Earth without its engines running. Is that because there's no gravity that high up, or because the Station has escaped Earth's gravity? If neither, what is actually keeping it up — and why doesn't it just fall down? Tell me WHY.
checkAnswer: There is still strong gravity at the Station's height — about 90% as strong as at Earth's surface — so it hasn't escaped gravity at all. The Station IS falling toward Earth constantly; it just moves sideways so fast (about 8 km per second) that as it falls, the curved Earth keeps curving away beneath it and it keeps 'missing' the ground. That continuous falling-while-missing IS an orbit (Newton's cannonball). The astronauts float because they are in the same continuous freefall as the Station, falling together — not because gravity is gone. No engine thrust is needed to stay in orbit, because nothing slows the sideways motion in the vacuum.
